guide.title: Musculoskeletal Injuries & Splinting
guide.lead: Splints ease pain, limit bleeding and protect nerves and vessels. Check circulation, movement and sensation before and after, immobilise above and below, and know which leg needs traction and which must never have it. Watch for compartment syndrome.

steps.title: CMS before
steps.text: Circulation, motor, sensation distal to the injury.

steps.title: Position
steps.text: Splint as found; one gentle realignment per protocol only if pulseless or impossible to transport.

steps.title: Above and below
steps.text: Joints above and below a fracture; bones above and below a joint.

steps.title: Pad and secure
steps.text: Open fracture: moist sterile dressing first; never push bone back.

steps.title: CMS after
steps.text: And after every move; cold pack wrapped in cloth.

sections.title: Leg deformity: traction or not?
rows: Thigh deformity and swelling, often shortened
Shortened, externally rotated; older adult after a fall
notes: No traction with knee, lower leg or ankle injury on the same side, or partial amputation.
Femur fracture can lose 1–1.5 L of blood.

quiz.q: Fall from a ladder: obvious mid-thigh deformity and swelling, leg shortened, CMS intact, no other injuries. Splint?
options: Traction splint for an isolated mid-shaft femur fracture; CMS before and after
quiz.explanation: Check for hip, pelvic and knee injuries first.

quiz.q: Open lower-leg fracture with bone showing:
options: Moist sterile dressing over the bone, splint as found, cold pack, transport

quiz.q: Deformed thigh, groin pain, tender pubic bone, flank bruising, HR 118. The crew wants a traction splint. Best action?
options: No traction: suspected pelvic injury – pelvic binder, rigid splint, trauma centre
quiz.explanation: A "stable" pelvis on exam doesn't rule out fracture.

quiz.q: Two hours after splinting a tibia: pain 10/10, pain on passive toe movement, pale tingling toes, weak pulse. Diagnosis and action?
options: Compartment syndrome: loosen the splint, limb at heart level, emergency transport for fasciotomy

quiz.q: Older woman, fell from standing: leg shortened and externally rotated, groin pain. Splint?
options: Padded immobilisation (pillows, vacuum mattress); no traction

quiz.q: Shortened, internally rotated, flexed leg after a dashboard impact:
options: Posterior hip dislocation: splint as found

quiz.q: Squared-off shoulder after a fall on an outstretched hand:
options: Anterior shoulder dislocation: sling and swathe, check deltoid sensation, don't reduce
quiz.explanation: Axillary nerve: sensation over the deltoid.

quiz.q: Before and after splinting, always check:
Which is a contraindication to a traction splint?
options: Ankle injury on the same leg

flashcards.question: Splinting principles
flashcards.answer: CMS before and after; splint as found; immobilise above and below; pad; cover open wounds; cold pack; reassess after every move.

flashcards.question: Signs of a fracture
flashcards.answer: Deformity, crepitus, swelling, bruising, point tenderness, loss of function, CMS changes.

flashcards.question: Closed vs open fracture
flashcards.answer: Closed: skin intact. Open: bone through the skin or a wound reaching the fracture; moist sterile dressing, never push bone back.

flashcards.question: Traction splint contraindications
flashcards.answer: Hip or pelvic fracture, hip dislocation, knee or lower leg/ankle injury on the same side, partial amputation.

flashcards.question: Compartment syndrome signs
flashcards.answer: Pain out of proportion and on passive stretch (early); paresthesia, pallor, paralysis, poikilothermia, pulselessness (late).

flashcards.question: Hip dislocation vs hip fracture
flashcards.answer: Posterior dislocation: shortened, internally rotated, flexed. Hip fracture: shortened, externally rotated. Neither gets traction.

flashcards.question: Anterior shoulder dislocation
flashcards.answer: Squared-off shoulder, arm held out and rotated outward. Sling and swathe, check deltoid sensation, don't reduce.

flashcards.question: Fasciotomy
flashcards.answer: Surgical release of a tight compartment: the treatment for compartment syndrome. Don't wait for pulselessness.

critical.scenario: A tackled 16-year-old has an obviously deformed, swollen mid-thigh, leg shortened, CMS intact, no other injuries. Your partner gets the traction splint.
critical.question: What must you verify and do?

options.t: Confirm an isolated mid-shaft femur fracture (no hip, pelvic, knee or lower leg injury), CMS, manual traction, apply the splint, CMS again, document
Apply it fast without checking: any leg deformity gets traction
options.f: Missing a hip or pelvic injury causes harm.

options.t: Pull until the leg is fully the same length

critical.explanation: A femur fracture can lose 1–1.5 L.
critical.kpi: Applies traction splint with correct indications and CMS checks

critical.scenario: An 18-year-old fell on an outstretched hand: squared-off shoulder, arm held away from the body, humeral head felt at the front. Normal deltoid sensation and radial pulse.
critical.question: Injury and management?

options.t: Anterior shoulder dislocation: sling and swathe as found, CMS including deltoid sensation, cold pack, transport; don't reduce

options.f: Not within EMS scope; risk of fracture or nerve injury.

critical.explanation: Recurrent dislocators may self-reduce: document it.
critical.kpi: Recognizes and immobilises an anterior shoulder dislocation

critical.scenario: Pinned 20 minutes by a forklift: open mid-tibia fracture splinted 30 minutes ago. Pain now unbearable, pale tingling toes, no foot pulse, screams on toe movement.
critical.question: Complication and immediate action?

options.t: Compartment syndrome: remove or loosen the splint and dressings, note the time pulses were lost, limb at heart level, emergency transport with pre-alert
Normal fracture pain: elevate the leg

critical.explanation: Crush mechanism: also watch for crush syndrome and high potassium.
